items_missed: Never asked 'how are you today?' — the opener went straight from 'Am I speaking with Oscar?' into 'I'm calling because we received your request for an estimate.'

Never checked availability for the move date. She read the date off the form ('you're moving on Thursday October 22nd') but never confirmed Einstein has that day open, which is the natural bridge to a booking attempt on a long-haul job that needs two crew-days.

No estimate was ever delivered. She gave the rate components — '$192 per hour for two movers and one truck,' 'a one time travel fee of $960 and an overnight fee of $240' — but never stated an estimated hour range or a ballpark total. On a call whose stated purpose was 'we received your request for an estimate,' the customer hung up without hearing a number, and had to ask for it: 'just send me the quote for the San antonio 18.'
No typical time range for a two-bedroom apartment, and the elevator/third-floor destination was captured but never explained as a time variable.

No Worries Damage Coverage never mentioned — the largest single miss on this call. She had told him herself 'we don't have box for the size of TV so we will just wrap it with our moving blankets' on an unboxed 75-inch TV going 200+ miles, and let that risk sit uncovered instead of answering it with the $2,000 coverage.
Meet Your Mover never mentioned — and this is a returning customer ('I used you guys about two years ago') where the mover-photo email is an easy trust win.
On-Time Guarantee never mentioned.

Full 'no hidden fees' pitch never delivered. She said 'everything is included in this hourly rate' and 'There's only two things outside of the hourly rate,' but never ran the no-credit-card-fees / no-transportation-fees / no-fuel-surcharge / no-assembly-fees list — the exact framing that defuses a fee objection before it lands.

'No deposit required' never mentioned. The customer's whole objection was fee-driven ('I think it's ridiculous that you guys are asking for an overnight fee') and the strongest no-risk lever Einstein has was left on the table.

Clock section almost entirely absent — no 'clock starts on-site when the contract opens,' no 2.5-hour minimum, no 15-minute prorated increments. Only the sense-check landed ('Does that make sense so far?'). On an hourly job with a $960 travel fee, the customer has no idea how the billable hours actually accrue.

Save Your Ass speech never delivered — 0 for the section, on the single best-set-up call for it. He volunteered 'I'm getting rid of a lot of stuff so, because I'm going from a two bedroom to a one bedroom' and dropped his own box estimate from 25-35 to 15-25. No 'prep before move day means a shorter move and a lower bill,' no consolidation examples, no 'take a carload.'
No booking attempt of any kind. No 'we have availability — want to lock that in?' The call ended as a quote-send with the customer saying 'I'm probably gonna use yell as a last resort.'

Confirmation email explained only as a delivery mechanism ('I'll send you an email to make sure your email is Oscar one oh, underscore 2000 @yahoo.com'). No BOLDED key-details framing, no 'reply with any corrections,' no hours or how to reach us.

Packing question asked and then abandoned. 'And do you need our help packing your small items in two boxes? Or will you be able to do it yourself?' — she said 'Okay' and moved to the next question without an answer on the transcript. Packing pricing (same hourly rate plus materials) was never quoted, so the estimate rests on an unconfirmed assumption.

The price objection was never handled. He objected twice — 'That's crazy to me that I'm that I'm having to pay for an overnight day' and 'I think it's ridiculous that you guys are asking for an overnight fee' — and got 'Just a second. Let me check' and 'Uh-huh. Mm-hmm.' No acknowledgment, no value reframe, no budget-conscious framing.

Two conflicting overnight explanations given inside two minutes. San Antonio version: 'they will stay overnight in a hotel in Houston and then they will drive back the next day.' Houston-booking version: 'they will keep it in our branch overnight and they will go to your new apartment the next day. To unload.' Those are materially different services — crew lodging versus the customer's goods sitting overnight — and the second one was delivered mid-fumble.
Customer's name used only twice, both in the first ten seconds ('Am I speaking with Oscar? Hi Oscar') — short of the 3+ standard, and never once during the objection when it would have mattered most.
Customer's mood clearly worsened over the call: opened cooperative ('Yeah. That's fine. I use I used you guys about two years ago') and closed with 'I'm probably gonna use yell as a last resort.'
Insurance never explained at all — no No Worries, no 60c/lb baseline.

Audible dead air and stalling during the objection: 'Just a second.' / 'Let me check if that will be.' / 'because hold on.' / 'Let me.' / 'Can.' / 'Checking how much will be the travel fee? Hold on.' Six fragments of hold-on with no bridging language.
top_strength: The discovery half of this call was genuinely strong and should be the model for the rest of the team. Nicole recapped the quote form back with real specificity — date, origin, destination, and 'almost three and a half to four hours drive between the location' — then worked a clean, complete probe: furniture inventory, TV boxing, appliances ('will there be any other appliances, like Washer/Dryer or fridge?'), additional spaces ('like from a balcony storage room or a garage?'), floor and walk distance at origin, floor and elevator at destination, additional stops, packing, and an explicit stressor ask: 'before I go over with our pricing structure and your estimate, do you have any specific concern or stresser about the moving process in general?' Two moves stood out. First, she calibrated the box count instead of accepting a guess: 'for a typical two bedroom apartment we usually expect to see around 25 to 35... do you think you'll follow within that range?' — and when he said less, she offered concrete brackets and got him to commit to fifteen to 25. That is exactly the estimate-accuracy behavior Einstein is trying to build. Second, she surfaced a problem proactively rather than letting it become a move-day surprise: 'just heads-up we don't have box for the size of TV so we will just wrap it with our moving blankets. Will that be fine?' She also caught the repeat-customer signal and thanked him for it — 'Thank you so much for choosing us again on your upcoming move.'
coaching_note: Highest-leverage fix: she never gave the estimate. Every input she needed was in hand — two-bedroom to one-bedroom, first floor to third floor with elevator, 15-25 boxes, 50-foot and 150-foot walks, no additional stops, no appliances — and then the call ended as a quote-send. After 'Does that make sense so far?' the next words should have been: 'So Oscar, for a two-bedroom apartment like yours with about 20 boxes, we typically see 5 to 7 hours of labor at $192 an hour for two movers and a truck, so roughly $960 to $1,344 in labor, plus the $960 travel fee and the $240 overnight — call it $2,200 to $2,500 all in, and there's no deposit to hold the date. I've got Thursday October 22nd open right now — want me to lock it in?' Say the number and ask for the business. Second priority: the overnight fee objection was the whole call and she never answered it. 'That's crazy to me that I'm having to pay for an overnight day' needed acknowledgment plus value, not a hold: 'I hear you, Oscar — nobody wants to see a line item they haven't seen before. What that $240 covers is a dedicated crew that loads your apartment in San Antonio and drives your things straight to Summer Street, no warehouse, no transfer to another truck, no shared load. Federal rules cap our drivers at ten hours, so the hotel night is what makes same-crew-door-to-door possible on a 200-mile move. And you're covered by our No Worries Damage Coverage the whole way — up to $2,000 to repair, replace, or reimburse — which matters for that 75-inch TV riding without its box.' That single answer pairs the objection, the differentiator, and the risk he already raised. Third: Save Your Ass was free money here and scored zero. He told her he is downsizing and purging. 'Since you're already getting rid of things, here's how to turn that into money off your bill: every box you have taped, labeled, and stacked by the front door when we walk in is time we're not paying for, and anything small enough to fit in your car should go in your car — pictures off the walls, loose drawer items, cleaning supplies. Customers who prep well routinely save an hour or two, which on this job is $200 to $400. Does that make sense?' Also fix the pricing-page fluency: six separate 'hold on' fragments while checking whether the Houston branch would be cheaper, then two contradictory overnight explanations, is what turned a fee question into a lost sale. Have the long-haul travel-fee logic for the San Antonio and Houston branches at hand before dialing any out-of-market lead. Business risk to close today: this is a returning customer who left saying he'd use Einstein 'as a last resort' — worth a follow-up call from Nhel or a manager with the full value pitch and the no-deposit line before he books elsewhere.
phone_presence_notes: Polite and structured with real warmth markers early ('Awesome,' 'Thank you so much for choosing us again'), but she met an openly frustrated customer with 'Uh-huh. Mm-hmm.' and six 'hold on' fragments, never acknowledged the emotion, and closed with a scripted 'You're welcome again, this is Nicole' after he had said he'd use Einstein as a last resort.
audio_review_reason: Score of 2 plus heavy transcription garbling in the load-bearing stretches ('around 25 to 35 pop back system of,' 'if we will book in used on,' 'a loud doc,' 'use yell as a last resort') — need audio to confirm whether the flat objection handling was genuinely flat delivery or a transcript artifact, and to judge how long the dead air during the Houston-branch lookup actually ran.
